deep.reconstruction:
This page continues Euler's discussion, begun on p.102, of the 'Fermat problem': find a rule that produces arbitrarily large primes. On p.102 Euler proved that no nonconstant integer polynomial X(x) takes only prime values. If X(a)=A, then for x = nA + a the value X(x) is divisible by A, since X(x) ≡ X(a) (mod A).

Here he weakens the demand. It would be enough to have a progression with infinitely many prime terms whose indices could be recognised. His example is a function f with f(x) prime whenever x is prime. He notes that this is equivalent to a rule that turns any given prime into a new prime. He judges such a rule 'of the deepest investigation' and sees no hope of solving Fermat's problem that way. He concludes that nothing has yet been achieved, since Fermat's own attempt (the conjecture that all 2^(2^n)+1 are prime) failed.

He then turns to the practical situation. Prime tables do not go beyond 100,000; a table to 101,000 has recently appeared. Exhibiting even one prime above that bound seems to need the ordinary sieve: strike out every number divisible by a prime below its square root. That amounts to extending the prime table itself, an 'immense' labour, and in his view nobody would carry it past a million.

This sets up the next page. There he introduces his special method based on numbers of the form a^2+1, whose odd prime divisors must be ≡ 1 (mod 4). That restriction makes trial division cheap and lets him certify primes above 10^6.
errors: No mathematical error. The pessimistic forecast that no table would ever pass one million was historically wrong: Felkel, Vega, Burckhardt and others did so later in the 18th and early 19th centuries.

The idea of a polynomial f with f(p) prime for every prime p is left as merely 'very hard'. It is in fact impossible for nonconstant f, but only via Dirichlet's theorem on primes in progressions applied to the p.102 argument. Euler does not see or state this.

ideas.what: Seek f such that f(p) is prime whenever p is prime, equivalently a rule mapping primes to new primes
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore; later Mills (1947), Wright, and others for non-polynomial prime-representing functions
ideas.where_published: E283 (this paper); related remarks in Euler's correspondence with Goldbach

ideas.what: Sieve of Eratosthenes: test divisibility only by primes up to the square root, as the standard way to extend prime tables
ideas.modern_name: sieve of Eratosthenes / trial division bound

ideas.what: State of prime tables in Euler's time: up to about 100,000, plus a recent table to 101,000 (presumably Krüger/Jäger, 1746)
ideas.modern_name: history of factor and prime tables

missed.claim: Combining Euler's p.102 divisibility argument (f(x) ≡ f(a) mod f(a) along x ≡ a) with primes in arithmetic progressions shows that no nonconstant polynomial maps all primes to primes. Euler poses the question but does not make this link; it is well known today.
missed.quote: quaerenda esset eiusmodi functio ipsius x, quae, quoties x fuerit numerus primus, ipsa quoque foret numerus primus
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Only of historical interest: an early posing of the prime-to-prime polynomial question. It is standard material now.

deep.surprise_reason: This is motivational, historical prose. The ideas are standard and well documented, and E283's a^2+1 method is known to Euler scholars.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image. The '10,1000' in the image is 101000.
